newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd Webber wine collection not going for a song.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd Webber wine collection not going for a song.

text.p: Andrew Lloyd Webber was selling his wine collection on Tuesday in an auction expected to fetch two million pounds ($3.3 million) and provide connoisseurs with the ingredients for a perfect millennium party.

When the Oscar-winning British composer was not writing hit musicals "Evita" and "Cats", he was putting together what Sotheby's describe as "the greatest single-owner wine collection ever to be offered at auction".
An incurable collector, he bought 18,000 bottles, which is more fine wine than anyone could ever drink.
"Wine is alive and now I realise I have been hogging far too much of it. It is time for a clear-out," Lloyd Webber says in the introduction to the sumptuously produced auction catalogue.

"Having said that, this is all a bit of a wrench. There's nothing I like more of an evening than a trip down to the cellar. Many is the time I've shut the big double doors with a 'bye bye boys' to my tannic pets."
Sotheby's describes the cellar offered at a two-day sale as the stuff of every connoisseur's dreams.
"It is a roll call of the most beautiful and perhaps the most opulent wines ever to be created," said Serena Sutcliffe, head of Sotheby's wine department.

The most spectacular lot in the sale is the "Millennium Cellar Super Lot", a selection of some of the greatest wines ever produced, ranging from Margaux 1900 to Corton Renardes 1990. It is expected to fetch up to 200,000 pounds.
Those determined to celebrate the millennium in style will also be drawn to the champagnes on offer.
"There are an awful lot of people just waiting to get their hands on the champagnes for the millennium," said Sutcliffe. "There is a feeling that it's going to be big."
Her own personal favourite is the Chateau d'Yquem 1900, expected to fetch up to 3,000 pounds a bottle.
If that doesn't appeal, there is Chateau Cheval Blanc 1947, described as a "vinous milestone of this century" and expected to sell for up to 30,000 pounds a case of 12 bottles.
Slightly cheaper from the same year is the Chateau Latour a Pomerol, estimated at up to 20,000 pounds a case and modestly described as "absolutely sensational".

Sutcliffe said buyers were expected from Britain, Germany, Switzerland and the Americas. Wine lovers were also emerging in the booming economies of the Pacific rim -- Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore and Japan.
There are also cheaper wines on sale, with cases of good white Burgundy at around 200 pounds.
"That's the kind of thing I'd go for and leave the billionaires to fight it out for the '47s," said Sutcliffe.
Lloyd Webber began his collection when he was at school and is selling some bottles of 1961 claret he bought for as little as one pound.
He has not given up the wine collecting habit. He's back in the market, this time buying young 1995 vintages from France and the New World.
